Header: Radopholus similis Kaponya nkonde in Bemba language; banana burrowing/toppling nematode

Prevention: Remove all weeds from banana fields because many of them can act as alternative hosts.
Use disease-free, certified, clean planting materials e.g., from tissue culture plants obtained from
Don't take suckers from other fields, which might be infested with nematodes.
Practice crop nutrition; in case of serious nematode infestation, consider fallows for 2-3 years to break the nematode cycle.
Plant old, local, tolerant varieties such as
Mbanda, Mwachusa, Nsenga; or plant new, tolerant varieties such as
The day before planting, place suckers in hot water, at 53-55°C for 20 minutes.
Apply mulch (e.g. by using dead grass material) to increase organic matter and stimulate root growth of bananas.
Apply sound crop nutrition, ideally, also manure, to increase vigour and help the plants withstand nematode attack.
Plant nematode-suppressing plants such as marigolds in the aisles of the plantation to reduce nematode populations.
Monitoring: Look out for single- stunted plants in a small holding or for spots of stunted plants in larger plantations.
Observe plants that grow slowly and reach fruiting stage late, which is due to limited root capacity to absorb water, due to nematode feeding.
Look for necrosis (lesions) at edges of cut roots or pseudostems of infested banana plants.
Check for falling over banana plants (especially older ones) and act when 3-5 plants/ha have fallen.
Direct Control: Destroy the pulled out rhizomes of the fallen plants
Spray chilli solution around the base of the remaining standing plants at a rate of 50mg/10 litres of water per plant.
Infested corms should have the outer layer peeled, and then be coated with azadirachtin.
Support infected plants with a wire or hooked post (or
Y- shaped stake) to prevent falling over to preserve harvestable crops.
